Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
Application of junction diode -diode as a rectifier.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Match each term of band theory in List-I with its description in List-II.

right: I. Range of energies in which no electron states are allowed
II. Vacancy in the valence band that acts like a positive charge carrier
III. Band above the gap, empty at 0 K in a pure semiconductor
IV. Band of levels of the outer electrons, completely filled at 0 K

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Which of the following arranges germanium (Ge), silicon (Si) and diamond (C) in order of increasing forbidden energy gap?

options.label: A
options.text: Si, Ge, diamond (about 1.1 eV, 0.7 eV, 5.4 eV)

options.label: B
options.text: Ge, diamond, Si (about 0.7 eV, 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV)

options.label: C
options.text: Diamond, Si, Ge (about 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV, 0.7 eV)

options.label: D
options.text: Ge, Si, diamond (about 0.7 eV, 1.1 eV, 5.4 eV)

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): At 0 K the valence band of a pure semiconductor is completely filled.
Reason (R): At 0 K the conduction band of a pure semiconductor is partially filled with electrons.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor at room temperature, which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: There are holes in the valence band but no electrons in the conduction band

options.label: B
options.text: The number of electrons in the conduction band equals the number of holes in the valence band

options.label: C
options.text: The number of electrons in the conduction band is much greater than the number of holes

options.label: D
options.text: The conduction band is completely full and the valence band is empty

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: The forbidden energy gap of silicon at room temperature is closest to which value?

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: In terms of energy bands, which description fits a metallic conductor such as copper?

options.label: A
options.text: The valence band is completely filled, the conduction band is empty and the gap between them is about 5 eV.

options.label: B
options.text: The valence band is completely filled, the conduction band is empty and the gap between them is about 1 eV.

options.label: C
options.text: The valence and conduction bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled), so there is no energy gap.

options.label: D
options.text: All the bands are completely filled, so electrons cannot gain energy from a field.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Which option correctly gives the sign of the temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal and of a pure semiconductor?

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: In a crystal, the band of energy levels occupied by the outermost (valence) electrons of the atoms at 0 K is called the

options.label: A
options.text: impurity band, which is present in every intrinsic semiconductor crystal

options.label: B
options.text: valence band, which is completely filled in an intrinsic semiconductor

options.label: C
options.text: forbidden gap, which can be occupied by electrons at 0 K if it is narrow enough

options.label: D
options.text: conduction band, which is completely filled at 0 K in an intrinsic semiconductor

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: In the band picture of a semiconductor, a hole is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: an extra electron in the conduction band that has a positive charge

options.label: B
options.text: a vacant state in the valence band that behaves like a mobile positive charge

options.label: C
options.text: a vacancy in the conduction band that carries a negative charge

options.label: D
options.text: an atom that has been removed from the crystal lattice

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Match each material in List-I with its band description in List-II.

right: I. Band gap about 5.4 eV
II. Valence and conduction bands overlap, no gap
III. Band gap about 1.1 eV
IV. Band gap about 0.7 eV

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: A photodetector responds to light of wavelengths up to a limit of 1.1 $\mu\text{m}$. What is the band gap of its semiconductor material in eV? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.)

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: As isolated atoms are brought closer to form a crystal, their energy levels spread into bands. Which statement about the width of the bands at the equilibrium spacing is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The levels do not broaden at all if the crystal has only a few atoms

options.label: B
options.text: All levels of the atom broaden by the same amount, as the spacing is the same

options.label: C
options.text: Outer (valence) levels broaden into wider bands than inner core levels, since their orbitals overlap more

options.label: D
options.text: Inner core levels broaden into wider bands than outer levels, since they are closer to the nuclei

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Pure diamond ($E_g \approx 5.4\,\text{eV}$) is transparent to visible light (wavelengths about 400 nm to 700 nm), while silicon ($E_g \approx 1.1\,\text{eV}$) absorbs it. Taking $hc = 1240\,\text{eV nm}$, which statement best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Visible photons carry more energy than diamond's band gap, so they pass straight through diamond.

options.label: B
options.text: Diamond's valence and conduction bands overlap, so it reflects visible light instead of absorbing it.

options.label: C
options.text: Visible photons carry about 1.8 eV to 3.1 eV, less than diamond's gap but more than silicon's, so they excite electrons in silicon but not in diamond.

options.label: D
options.text: Silicon's band gap is larger than the energy of visible photons, so silicon absorbs them.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The resistivity of a metal such as copper increases when its temperature is raised.
Reason (R): In a metal, the number of free electrons increases rapidly as the temperature rises.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: At 300 K the typical thermal energy $k_BT$ is only about 0.026 eV, yet pure silicon ($E_g \approx 1.1\,\text{eV}$) has a measurable number of conduction electrons at room temperature. Which statement best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The band gap of silicon shrinks to about 0.026 eV at room temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Thermal energies are spread over a range; a tiny fraction of the enormous number of valence electrons have energies many times $k_BT$, enough to cross the gap.

options.label: C
options.text: Electrons cross the gap by stepping through allowed levels that exist inside the forbidden gap of pure silicon.

options.label: D
options.text: At room temperature every silicon atom gives up one valence electron to the conduction band.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Optical-fibre links commonly use infrared light of wavelength $1.5\,\mu\text{m}$. A detector works only if each photon can lift an electron across the band gap of its material. Which of these materials can detect this light? Take $hc = 1240\,\text{eV nm}$.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: A light-emitting diode is made from a semiconductor of band gap 2.0 eV. When an electron falls across the gap and recombines with a hole, the energy is emitted as a photon. What is the wavelength of the light emitted? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.)

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Magnesium has a completely filled valence band in the free-atom picture (two electrons in the 3s level), yet it is a good conductor. How do energy bands explain this?

options.label: A
options.text: Magnesium has a wide gap that thermal energy easily bridges at 300 K

options.label: B
options.text: The forbidden gap in magnesium is exactly zero in width at every temperature

options.label: C
options.text: The valence band overlaps the next empty band, so electrons can move into available states

options.label: D
options.text: The electrons are bound to the lattice so strongly that they cannot move

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: A semiconductor has a forbidden gap of 1.8 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light that can create electron-hole pairs in it? (Take $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.)

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Why does perfectly pure silicon behave as an insulator at 0 K?

options.label: A
options.text: Its band gap becomes larger than 3 eV at 0 K.

options.label: B
options.text: Its valence band is completely filled and its conduction band completely empty, and no thermal energy is available to lift electrons across the gap.

options.label: C
options.text: All its electrons are in the conduction band but they cannot move at 0 K.

options.label: D
options.text: Its valence and conduction bands overlap at 0 K, so the electrons are trapped.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Silicon is a semiconductor, whereas diamond, which has a similar crystal structure, is an insulator.
Reason (R): The forbidden energy gap of diamond is much larger than that of silicon.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about energy bands.
A. In metals the conduction band is partly filled or overlaps the valence band.
B. In semiconductors the forbidden gap is small, of the order of 1 eV or so.
C. In insulators the forbidden gap is large, greater than about 3 eV.
D. In semiconductors the number of free charge carriers decreases as the temperature rises.
Choose the correct option.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the formation of energy bands in a crystal of N identical atoms.
A. Each atomic energy level splits into N closely spaced levels.
B. The levels of inner-shell electrons broaden much more than those of the outermost electrons.
C. In a perfect crystal there are no allowed electron energy levels inside the forbidden gap.
D. The splitting happens because the Pauli exclusion principle does not allow two electrons of the crystal to occupy the same quantum state.
Which of the statements are correct?

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Germanium has a band gap of about 0.7 eV and silicon about 1.1 eV. At the same temperature, which statement about the pure crystals is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither has any electron-hole pairs, since the gap is greater than the thermal energy

options.label: B
options.text: Both have equal numbers of electron-hole pairs, since the temperature is the same

options.label: C
options.text: Silicon has more electron-hole pairs, because its larger gap lets more electrons cross

options.label: D
options.text: Germanium has more electron-hole pairs, because its smaller gap is crossed more easily

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: In a crystal of N silicon atoms (outer configuration $3s^2\,3p^2$), the 3s and 3p levels regroup into two bands separated by a gap. At 0 K, the lower of these two bands:

options.label: A
options.text: contains 4N states and is completely filled by the 4N valence electrons

options.label: B
options.text: contains 8N states and is half filled by the 4N valence electrons

options.label: C
options.text: contains 2N states and is completely filled, leaving 2N electrons in the upper band

options.label: D
options.text: contains 4N states but only 2N of them are occupied

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The resistivity of a pure semiconductor decreases as its temperature increases.
Reason (R): At higher temperature more electrons are excited across the band gap into the conduction band, increasing the number of free electrons and holes available for conduction.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Refer to panel (a) of the figure. Why can the material shown in panel (a) conduct electricity even at 0 K?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the overlapping bands leave the highest-energy electrons with empty levels immediately above them, so no thermal energy is needed for them to respond to a field.

options.label: B
options.text: Because its band gap is about 1 eV, which electrons can cross easily even at 0 K.

options.label: C
options.text: Because holes are created in its valence band by thermal excitation at 0 K.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the overlap region acts as a forbidden gap that stores electrons until a field is applied.

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: N identical atoms are brought together to form a crystal. The band that forms from the 3s level of the atoms can hold at most how many electrons?

options.label: A
options.text: 2N, because N levels each hold two electrons of opposite spin

options.label: B
options.text: 4N, because each level holds electrons of both spin and both signs

options.label: C
options.text: 6N, because the band includes three sub-levels of each atom

options.label: D
options.text: N, because each level in the band holds only one electron

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: Three crystals X, Y and Z have forbidden gaps of 1.1 eV, 2.4 eV and 5.4 eV respectively. Red light of wavelength 700 nm (photon energy about 1.8 eV) falls on each. In which crystal can the photons create electron-hole pairs?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in X, since 1.8 eV exceeds its gap but not the other two

options.label: B
options.text: Only in Y, since its gap is the closest above the photon energy

options.label: C
options.text: In all three, since light of any wavelength can excite electrons

options.label: D
options.text: In both X and Y, since both gaps are less than twice the photon energy

questions.unit: Energy bands in conductors, semiconductors and insulators (qualitative ideas only).
questions.stem: The band gap of germanium is 0.7 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light that can create electron-hole pairs in germanium? Take $hc = 1240\,\text{eV nm}$.

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: The threshold (knee) voltage of a silicon junction diode, beyond which the forward current rises sharply, is about:

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: A p-n junction diode is said to be forward biased when it is connected with:

options.label: A
options.text: its p-side to the positive terminal and its n-side to the negative terminal of the battery

options.label: B
options.text: its p-side to the negative terminal and its n-side to the positive terminal of the battery

options.label: C
options.text: both its sides to the positive terminal of the battery

options.label: D
options.text: its p-side to the battery and its n-side left unconnected

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: In the circuit symbol of a junction diode, what does the arrowhead indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: It points from the n-side to the p-side, the direction in which electrons flow in forward bias

options.label: B
options.text: It shows the direction of the reverse saturation current through the diode

options.label: C
options.text: It shows the direction of the electric field in the depletion region

options.label: D
options.text: It points from the p-side (anode) to the n-side (cathode), the direction of conventional current in forward bias

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: Which one of the following impurities, added in a small amount to pure silicon, produces an n-type semiconductor?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: For a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium, whether intrinsic or doped, the product $n_e n_h$ of the electron and hole densities is equal to:

options.label: C
options.text: nᵢ², the square of the intrinsic carrier concentration

options.label: D
options.text: zero, because electrons and holes recombine

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor at room temperature, how does the free-electron density $n_e$ compare with the hole density $n_h$?

options.label: A
options.text: The electron density is greater than the hole density

options.label: B
options.text: The electron density is equal to the hole density

options.label: C
options.text: The electron density is less than the hole density

options.label: D
options.text: Both are zero at room temperature

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: The depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction contains:

options.label: C
options.text: equal numbers of free electrons and holes

options.label: D
options.text: immobile donor and acceptor ions, with practically no mobile charge carriers

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem:
Consider these statements about the I-V characteristics of a p-n junction diode.
A. The forward current (beyond the knee) is mainly due to diffusion of majority carriers across the lowered barrier.
B. The reverse current (below breakdown) is mainly due to drift of minority carriers.
C. Below the threshold voltage the forward current is negligibly small.
D. In reverse bias below breakdown, the current increases in direct proportion to the applied voltage, as Ohm's law predicts.
Which statements are correct?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: Two identical silicon diodes, both forward biased, are connected in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor across a 6.0 V battery. Taking the forward drop of each diode as 0.7 V, what is the current in the circuit?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: A germanium sample at 300 K has $n_i = 2.4\times10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$. After doping, its hole density is found to be four times its electron density. What are the electron density $n_e$ and hole density $n_h$?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: A 5.0 V battery, a 1.0 kΩ resistor and two identical silicon diodes D1 and D2 are connected in series. D1 is connected so that it is forward biased, but D2 is connected the opposite way round. What is the current in the circuit, approximately?

options.label: D
options.text: Practically zero (only the tiny reverse saturation current of D2)

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): When a p-n junction diode is reverse biased, no current at all flows through it.
Reason (R): Reverse bias raises the potential barrier, which almost stops the diffusion of majority carriers across the junction.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: A silicon p-n junction has a barrier potential of 0.7 V. It is forward biased with 0.4 V. A conduction electron on the n-side moves towards the junction with a kinetic energy of 1.0 eV. With what kinetic energy does it arrive on the p-side (ignore collisions)?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: A germanium p-n junction has a barrier potential of 0.3 V across a depletion region 0.2 µm wide. What is the average electric field in the depletion region?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): An n-type semiconductor is electrically neutral as a whole.
Reason (R): In an n-type semiconductor, the number of free electrons is equal to the number of holes.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: When a p-n junction is forward biased, what happens to the height of the potential barrier and the width of the depletion layer?

options.label: A
options.text: The barrier height increases and the depletion layer widens

options.label: B
options.text: The barrier height decreases and the depletion layer narrows

options.label: C
options.text: The barrier height decreases but the depletion layer widens

options.label: D
options.text: Neither the barrier height nor the depletion width changes

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The reverse saturation current of a junction diode increases when its temperature rises.
Reason (R): The depletion region of a junction diode widens when the reverse bias voltage is increased.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: When a p-n junction is formed and reaches equilibrium with no external voltage applied, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Only diffusion occurs, and it continues until all the holes have crossed to the n-side

options.label: B
options.text: Diffusion of majority carriers sets up a field that causes drift of minority carriers; at equilibrium the diffusion and drift currents are equal and opposite

options.label: C
options.text: Only drift occurs, because the barrier field exists before the junction is formed

options.label: D
options.text: A steady current flows from p to n through the junction even without a battery

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: When pure silicon is doped with phosphorus, what happens to its hole concentration (at the same temperature)?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases, because each phosphorus atom also creates a hole

options.label: B
options.text: It remains equal to nᵢ, because doping affects only electrons

options.label: C
options.text: It becomes exactly zero, because donor electrons fill every hole

options.label: D
options.text: It falls below nᵢ, because the extra electrons recombine with holes more often

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: In a p-type semiconductor, what are the majority charge carriers, and what kind of immobile ions are present in the lattice?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: What happens when the reverse voltage across an ordinary junction diode is increased up to its breakdown voltage?

options.label: A
options.text: The diode automatically switches over to forward bias

options.label: B
options.text: The reverse current drops to exactly zero

options.label: C
options.text: The depletion layer disappears and the barrier returns to 0.7 V

options.label: D
options.text: The reverse current increases sharply, and the diode can be damaged by overheating unless the current is limited

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: In the I-V characteristic shown, beyond the knee (about 0.7 V) a small increase in forward voltage produces a large increase in current. What does this tell you about the diode's dynamic resistance in this region?

options.label: A
options.text: It is very large, of the order of megaohms

options.label: B
options.text: It is small, typically a few ohms, and it decreases as the current increases

options.label: C
options.text: It is constant at all voltages, so the diode obeys Ohm's law

options.label: D
options.text: It is negative, because the current falls as the voltage rises

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: Why are dopant atoms for silicon chosen to be roughly the same size as silicon atoms, and added only in tiny amounts (about one part per million)?

options.label: A
options.text: So that they replace silicon atoms without distorting the crystal, while still supplying far more carriers than the intrinsic concentration

options.label: B
options.text: So that the band gap of silicon is reduced to zero, making it a metal

options.label: C
options.text: So that the dopant atoms form a separate metallic layer that carries the current

options.label: D
options.text: So that the numbers of electrons and holes remain exactly equal after doping

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: Silicon is doped with a pentavalent impurity so that the donor concentration is $1.0\times10^{22}\,\text{m}^{-3}$. If $n_i = 1.5\times10^{16}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, what is the hole concentration in the doped crystal?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a semiconductor, the motion of a hole in one direction is really the motion of bound valence electrons in the opposite direction.
Reason (R): A hole moves when an electron from a neighbouring covalent bond jumps into the vacancy, leaving a new vacancy at the bond it came from.

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: The figure shows an unbiased p-n junction with its depletion region and potential profile. Which statement about the electric field in the depletion region and the potentials of the two sides is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The field points from the n-side to the p-side, and the n-side is at the higher potential

options.label: B
options.text: The field points from the p-side to the n-side, and the p-side is at the higher potential

options.label: C
options.text: The field points from the n-side to the p-side, but the p-side is at the higher potential

options.label: D
options.text: There is no field, because the junction as a whole is electrically neutral

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: When the forward voltage across a silicon diode is increased from 0.70 V to 0.72 V, the current increases from 10 mA to 20 mA. What is the dynamic resistance of the diode in this range?

questions.unit: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-type and n-type, p-n junction Semiconductor
questions.stem: The small current that flows through a reverse-biased p-n junction (below breakdown) is mainly due to:

options.label: A
options.text: drift of minority carriers across the junction under the field

options.label: B
options.text: diffusion of majority carriers across a lowered barrier
